title: Don't insult their gods
hook: don't insult what others call on, lest they insult Allah in ignorance (6:108)

segments.voice: Yesterday: adraka, no vision grasps Him. Your line was seen by the unseen. Did you remember it when no one was watching? Today, a verse about the words we use for what other people hold sacred. Day four hundred three.

Every comment section on the internet runs on the same engine. Someone mocks a thing another person loves. The other person mocks something back, a little harder. Within a few replies, both sides are saying things about each other's most sacred things that neither would say to a face. Nobody's mind has changed. Everyone is angrier. Surah six was revealed in Mecca, when the Muslims were a small group surrounded by people who worshipped idols, and the arguments were real and daily. You might expect the Qur'an to sharpen their tongues. Verse one-oh-eight does the opposite.
screen: `THE COMMENT SECTION ENGINE.` → `MOCKED, AND MOCKED BACK.` → `MECCA, A SMALL GROUP.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “Revile not those unto whom they pray beside Allah lest they wrongfully revile Allah through ignorance.” The verb is sabba: to insult, to curse, to abuse with words. Notice what the verse does not say. It doesn't say the Qur'an has stopped disagreeing with idol worship; this same surah argues against it again and again, with stars and seeds and reasons. What it forbids is the insult. Disagree, explain, argue in the best way, as surah sixteen puts it: with wisdom and good counsel. But don't revile. And the reason is practical: insult what they call on, and they may revile Allah in return, out of ignorance. The verse goes on: to every community We have made their own deeds seem fair to them, and they will return to their Lord, who will tell them what they used to do. In other words, people hold dear what seems fair to them. Mock it, and the mockery comes back aimed at what you hold dear. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim works the same way. The Prophet ﷺ said one of the gravest sins is cursing your own parents. The companions asked, who would curse their own parents? He said: you insult another man's father, and he insults yours. Scholars built a principle from verses and hadith like these, sadd adh-dhara'i': closing the doors that lead to harm. Something permitted in itself can become forbidden when it reliably leads somewhere worse. A rude joke about someone else's faith is one of those doors.
screen: `SABBA — TO INSULT, TO REVILE.` · `DISAGREE, YES. INSULT, NO.` · `THEY'LL INSULT YOURS BACK.` · `CLOSE THE DOOR TO HARM.` · then, large: `REVILE NOT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a faith or a practice that isn't yours, one you've joked about, or heard joked about. Picture a real person who holds it dear: a grandmother, a classmate, a neighbor. See their face when it's mocked. Now think of one respectful sentence you could say about their faith, something true, said the way you'd want yours spoken of. Hold that sentence until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Sabba, to insult, to revile with words. Surah six, verse one-oh-eight: revile not what others call on, or they'll revile Allah in ignorance. Today's word.
Your line: don't insult. Today, if someone else's faith comes up, speak of it with respect, even where you disagree. Day four hundred three.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite 6:108 to forbid mocking what others hold sacred, and use it as a classic example of sadd adh-dhara'i', blocking the means to harm; some imams quote it in interfaith settings.

myth: 6:108 means Muslims may not disagree with other beliefs
the surah argues against idol worship often. it forbids insult, not disagreement.
the verse was revealed when Muslims were a small group in Mecca
a hadith says insulting another's father is a way of cursing your own
he insults yours in return (Bukhari and Muslim).

fork.setup: you're with friends, and someone starts mocking a neighbor's religion. what does 6:108's logic suggest?
options: join in. it's only a joke.
don't join the insult; disagree, if you must, with respect.
mock theirs back to balance it.
fork.reveal: revile not, lest they revile Allah in ignorance. the verse forbids insult and leaves room for respectful disagreement.

original.note: Arabic: and do not insult (6:108), from sabba, to revile.

trapdoor: what you thought: be polite about other religions.
what it means: disagreement is allowed; insult is not, because it closes hearts and invites insult of Allah in return.
what a scholar hears: jurists like al-Qurtubi cite 6:108 for sadd adh-dhara'i': a permitted act becomes forbidden when it leads to a greater harm.
